title: In a New Role, Achieve Clarity With a Don't Do List
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article advises leaders entering a new role to clarify success criteria and expectations before acting. Asking what others want done and how quickly yields a useful to-do list, but the author argues a second question set is more powerful: what shouldn't I do, get involved with, or change. The resulting Don't Do list shows how others define the role and exposes sacred cows, areas of strength and protected territories. The move is to listen and reserve judgment, then decide whether each item is defensiveness or sound advice. The piece recommends pairing both lists with critical stakeholders for sharper role clarity.
points: Leaders in a new role should define success criteria and expectations before jumping in, starting with a direct question about what others expect.
Asking what not to do, get involved with or change reveals how others see the role, not just the outcomes they want.
A Don't Do list surfaces sacred cows, existing strengths and territories that others protect.
The leader's discipline is to listen without committing, then judge each item as defensive posture or sound advice.
Together the Do and Don't Do lists give more precise clarity than the Do list alone.
quotes: When taking on a new role, position, or assignment, good leaders do everything they can to define the criteria of success and to understand the expectations others have of them before they jump into the fray.

Point blank asking what the team and the leaders above them expect helps to create important clarity. The compound question, “What would you like me to do and how quickly would you like me to do it?” sets the stage for understanding what others expect.

But there is another question set that is even more powerful for creating role clarity and it produces a very different pathway forward. Asking others “What shouldn’t I do?” “What shouldn’t I get involved with?” and “What shouldn’t I change?” will produce an entirely different level of understanding.

This Don’t Do list reveals how others see the role, not just what outcomes they expect. Learning what the team, customers, and peers think a leader should not tackle tells them oodles about how they define leadership success. More importantly, it exposes sacred cows, areas of strength, and territories protected by others.

Leaders listen and learn from the Don’t Do list and reserve judgment as to how they will proceed. When others tell a leader what boxes to ignore or not to check, they inadvertently describe how they see value in the role. Smart leaders dissect this information and decide whether what they have learned constitutes a defensive posture or sound advice.
The Don’t Do list creates a clarity of role that can’t be achieved by the Do list alone.
